expectations.text: In the source list, peer-reviewed research comes before weaker kinds of source such as news articles or preprints (within each group, if the list is grouped).
expectations.evidence: Sources 1–7 are listed under "Peer-reviewed articles" first, then "Preprint, not yet peer reviewed" (8), then "Research organization reports" (9–10).

expectations.text: Any news article, preprint, or other source that isn't peer-reviewed research comes with a plain reason why it's included or what to watch for. If there are none, this passes.
expectations.evidence: The preprint gives a reason ("I'm including it because it's the closest study to your second sub-question") and RAND has a caveat ("This is the press release; the full report (RRA4742-1) blocked me"), but the Pew report (#9) has only a summary, with no reason for including it and nothing to watch for.

expectations.text: The reply says which sources (or how many) meet the assignment's requirement of at least 3 peer-reviewed sources.
expectations.evidence: "All seven count toward your requirement of at least 3 peer-reviewed sources."

expectations.text: The reply does not show the user a rubric, a credibility score or rating (for example "7/10" or "Tier 2"), or named levels such as "strong evidence," "usable with care," or "not evidence on its own" presented as a rating system.
expectations.evidence: No scores, tiers, or named rating levels appear; sources are labeled only by type ("Peer-reviewed article", "Preprint", "Research organization reports").

expectations.text: Every link or DOI in the reply points to a page the transcript shows Claude opened (fetched) during this session.
expectations.evidence: The reply contains no DOIs. Its links (PMC12232635, arxiv 2412.09315, epub.ub.uni-muenchen.de/125262, arxiv 2409.09047, Pew, RAND) were each opened, either by WebFetch or by a Bash curl call.

expectations.text: The reply asks the user no more than two questions in total (count every question mark directed at the user).
expectations.evidence: The "Questions these results raise" section puts three questions to the user: "How well do findings about college students apply to high schoolers?", "Is 'checking your work' something students choose...?", and "Do the meta-analyses' positive averages hide differences...?"
